questions.q: A customer's billing system lists them in "NY" and the shipping system lists the same customer in "New York." Both values are individually valid. Which dimension is failing?
options: Consistency — the same fact disagrees with itself across systems
Validity — neither value conforms to a format rule
Completeness — a value is missing
Uniqueness — the customer appears twice
questions.explain: Consistency asks whether the same real-world fact, stored in more than one place, says the same thing everywhere — here it doesn't, even though both individual values are valid.

questions.q: An order_status column that should only contain Pending, Shipped, Cancelled, or Returned has a row with the value "Shipp3d." Which dimension is this?
options: Validity — it doesn't conform to the defined set of allowed values
Timeliness — the status is out of date
Accuracy — it doesn't match a real-world fact
Consistency — it disagrees with another system
questions.explain: Validity is about conforming to a defined format, type, or allowed set of values — a typo like "Shipp3d" is exactly what a CHECK constraint or validity rule should catch.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why can a stricter validity rule on phone number format actually hurt a different dimension?
options: It can reject legitimate international numbers, leaving the field blank and hurting completeness
It always improves every other dimension at the same time
Stricter rules have no effect on any other dimension
It makes the data more accurate automatically
questions.explain: The six dimensions can conflict — a format rule that's too strict trades validity gains for completeness losses when it rejects legitimate but differently-formatted values.

questions.q: A warehouse inventory count is accurate, complete, consistent, valid, and unique, but was last refreshed 18 hours ago, causing the business to oversell a product. Which dimension failed?
options: Timeliness
Accuracy
Uniqueness
Validity
questions.explain: Timeliness asks whether data is current enough for the decision being made with it right now — everything else about the data can be correct and it still fails this dimension.

questions.q: Two separate signup forms each create a record for "John Smith," splitting his purchase history across two rows. Which dimension is this?
options: Uniqueness — one real-world entity should appear exactly once
Completeness — a field is missing
Validity — a format rule was violated
Timeliness — the records are stale
questions.explain: Uniqueness asks whether each real-world entity is represented by exactly one row; duplicate customer records violate it even when every individual field is otherwise fine.
